items.title: Fishermen Miraculously Spot Cruise Ship Pianist Who Spent 9 Hours in Open Sea After Falling Overboard
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "I thought I was gonna die."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Sean Norton and Grant Garrett were fishing for marlin near Catalina Island off the coast of Los Angeles when they spotted something floating in the water. That something, though, turned out to be a someone.

The men, returning from a morning fishing trip, spotted the man on Nov. 6. The man treading water in the Pacific Ocean identified himself as a Royal Caribbean employee, a pianist, who had fallen overboard from the ship he was working on, CBS LA reported.

They found — and rescued — the man about 20 miles off the coast in the middle of the ocean.

“I’m like, ‘Yeah, it’s a human being. Stop the boat; let’s get all of our lines in,'” Garrett recalled. Norton said, “Grant and I each got an arm and lifted him up,” adding, “The only thing he said to me was, ‘Thank you. I thought I was gonna die.”

Garrett and Norton called for emergency assistance and Newport Beach lifeguards responded to help them. Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told the local CBS News affiliate they believe the Ovation of the Seas musician likely fell off the ship about nine hours earlier, at around 2:30 a.m.

The man, whose name hasn’t been disclosed, was transported to the Orange County Global Medical Center for care and is expected to make a miraculous recovery, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.

“You have this crazy super El Niño year,” said Norton. “This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water’s 76 degrees. A different year, no way he makes it.”

A spokesperson for Royal Caribbean said, “We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share.”

When Norton and Garrett pulled the man out, Norton remembered he was clearly in shock and said the only words he spoke were, “Thank you; I thought I was gonna die.”

items.title: Ezekiel 37 Prophecy About Israel’s Return Sparks Colton Dixon’s Latest Hit
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Interesting.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Singer Colton Dixon’s new song “Bones” comes at a time when the world feels, in many ways, like it’s on fire. The catchy tune is inspired by the valley of dry bones prophecy in Ezekiel 37.

Many Bible experts believe this chapter references Israel’s return to the land in 1948, and Dixon — who agrees — told CBN News some of his other reasons for connecting these Scriptures to “Bones.”

“It was kind of like the… the push to get off the sidelines as a believer, and to start prophesying over the dead things in my life,” he said of the song’s inspiration. “It comes from Ezekiel 37. … God gives Ezekiel a vision, brings him out into the middle of a desert full of a valley of dry bones, and tells him to start prophesying.”

Dixon continued, “So, as Ezekiel starts to prophesy, the bones start to rattle, they come together, and a whole army stands up around him.”

The singer believes the moment was prophetic for Israel “coming back and regaining their stance.” But he said the meaning can also run deeper, noting that Ezekiel’s hard-hitting message inspired him.

“As a believer, I’m like, ‘Man, I feel like we have this authority, spiritually, to prophesy over the dead things in our life,'” he said. “Galatians talks … about God getting us the keys to the kingdom. Whatever we bind on earth shall be bound in heaven. Whatever we loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. So I’m like, ‘All right, it’s time to stop sitting on the sidelines as a believer.'”

Dixon said it’s easy for Christians to fall into what he described as an “autopilot lifestyle” — something he wants to help people navigate.

“That’s not the way God designed it,” he said, comparing it to a car’s autopilot feature. “It’s a great feature for your car, I might add, but that’s not the way God designed us to … live our lives. You’re just going to miss out on God’s best for you doing it that way.”

He’s hoping “Bones” gets people thinking more about the importance of living out biblical truth.

“God has something incredible for you,” Dixon said. “And I don’t want to settle for…bad or good when I can have God’s best.”

items.title: Sadie Robertson Huff Was the Poster Child for Christianity. She Says It Nearly Crushed Her.
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: Sadie Robertson Huff spent years believing she had to be perfect for God and for her audience. She says a bare-faced video and one night in her backyard changed that.
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

By her teens, Sadie Robertson Huff had been cast as something she never auditioned for. Huff grew up on camera, on A&E’s Duck Dynasty, in a family that lived its faith out loud, and viewers took the teenager at the center of it as the model Christian girl. She says she felt every bit of that expectation.

“I was put in this position to be this poster child for Christianity,” she said. “I’m in this Christian family. They’re all living boldly for their faith. I need to be this good example. And yet the pressure of that felt so crippling because I wasn’t living that way.”

The gap between the image and the girl got filled with performance. Huff says she kept showing viewers the version they wanted.

“Instead of just being honest and being vulnerable and being authentic and saying I struggle, I was trying to be what people were projecting on me.”

That began to change with her first YouTube video. She posted it with wet hair and no makeup, which was a bigger statement then than it sounds now, and told viewers they had it wrong.

“Hey, I’m Sadie Robertson, and here’s what my life looks like. A lot of you guys keep saying I’m goals, but I’m really struggling. I feel really insecure. I have a lot of anxiety.”

It was the first time she let the audience see the person underneath. The poster-child pressure had followed her into her prayer life, though.

“I felt like I had to be perfect for him to be proud of me. I had to be perfect to stay in right relationship. And when I wasn’t perfect, because no one is, and I definitely struggled a whole lot, then I would just distance myself from him. When you’re struggling, that’s when you need to draw near. But when I’m struggling, I’m like, ‘I gotta get it together so that I can come near.'”

The video changed how she showed up online. The private version came later, after she had kids. She was behind at work, exhausted and sure she was failing at all of it. One night, after putting the children to bed, she went outside to tell God she was sorry she just couldn’t keep up.

“I walked outside to have some quiet time, and it was like a freight train of God’s grace hit me. I had no anticipation of feeling weight lifted. I had all the anticipation for repentance. I was going to say, ‘Lord, I’m dropping the ball in every area.’ And yet I sat there and I just felt God’s embrace and I just cried. I came back in to my husband and I said, ‘That was the craziest experience. I thought He was gonna be mad at me, but He just loved me.'”

She admits it sounds hard to explain. “I can’t explain it other than it was like an embrace,” she says. “I just felt a weight lifted.” Since then she’s been on a mission to tell people that God is more gracious, more kind and more loving than they think.

Huff keeps returning to the woman at the well to explain what happened to her. She has heard John 4 preached all her life, she says, and rereading it, she noticed what the woman chose to say when she ran back to town.

“Come meet a man who told me everything I ever did. That was the testimony. And that revelation of this man knows me, and he was willing to sit with me, and he was willing to drink from my cup, that he actually loves me.”

Her new book, It’s Not Personal, is built on the same story.

The comparison has a Christian version, too. Huff says she and her husband guard against it.

“One thing as a culture we have created in the Church sometimes is that competitive spirit of who gave the best message at the conference, who did the best worship set. Christian and I are like, we cannot let our mind go there. Don’t pay that attention, because it does something to your heart. Then you’re striving. I gotta bring my best. It’s gotta be better than I was last year.”

The expectations that came with being a poster child have not gone away. Every time Huff has been in what she calls the storms of social media, she says, the criticism has come from the Church, never from the secular world. When criticism from fellow Christians piled up online, including over a TikTok dance, she dreaded the next Sunday.

“I felt nervous to go to my church, because I felt like everybody’s seen this on Facebook, everybody’s seen this on Instagram and TikTok, and I just didn’t want to feel eyes on me,” she said. “I felt sad about it, I felt hurt by it. And so Christian and I were like, ‘Hey, it’s okay. We just need to go.’

“I was trying to slip out to go help one of my kids, and one of the elders just walked up to me and said, ‘Hey, I just want to encourage you. God is using you in such a mighty way.’ He didn’t bring up the controversy. I’m sure he saw it, based off of just how kind he was being, but he just spoke so much truth in my life. And I just was thinking, I’m so grateful that I came to church.”

She says she never wants to bash the Church. She’s had hate from it and so much love, she says, and she believes in it deeply. Her request is for the people who treat the internet as a separate place.

“We all have social media. I’m seeing you react to me. I’m scrolling, it’s in my algorithm. And so don’t take the humanity out of people on the other side of the screen. It matters so much that you’re loving them just as much.”

The criticism has also followed a harder question. Huff preaches, and she didn’t grow up in a church that allowed women to. Her family wrestled with it before she said yes, she says, reading through the scriptures and asking big questions, and she is grateful they did. The comments arrive anyway.

“People comment all kinds of stuff. ‘Sit down, shut up, you are feelings based, emotion based.’ I’ve seen the comments. I’ve seen the things. But I go back to what I know to be true and what the Lord has spoken, and what I’ve read and studied and people spoke into my life. It’s hurtful, it’s sad.”

What carries her through it, she says, is something Shelley Giglio once told her.

“Life is gonna be hard, but you’re looking for assurance that it’s what the Lord told you to do. Because if you have assurance, then you’ll be able to get through the hard.”

It is a long way from the girl who believed she had to get it together before she could come near to God.

items.title: Veterans Remind Us Who We Are
items.author: Dr. Tod Worner
items.summary:
Dr. Tod Worner

We thank all veterans—for giving their freedom to protect ours, for living with honor to preserve ours, for enduring the darkness so we may live in the light.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Tod Worner

Every man has forgotten who he is. . . . We are all under the same mental calamity; we have all forgotten our names. We have all forgotten what we really are.

—G. K. Chesterton

It is the unconquerable soul of man and not the nature of the weapon he uses which insures victory.

—Gen. George S. Patton

On June 5, 1944, a United States general strode on a platform donning a spit-shined helmet, polished cavalry boots, and a menacing riding crop in hand. Standing at attention were the United States Third Army’s Sixth Armored Division who were based in Gloucestershire, England, and preparing for the coming landings on Normandy beach. The hour to confront the Nazis in fortress Europe was at hand. And their leader stood before them. That man was Gen. George S. Patton.

The men were seated. The general paced. And glowered.

Men, this stuff that some sources sling around about America wanting out of this war, not wanting to fight, is a crock of bull—. Americans love to fight, traditionally. All real Americans love the sting and clash of battle. You are here today for three reasons. First, because you are here to defend your homes and your loved ones. Second, you are here for your own self respect, because you would not want to be anywhere else. Third, you are here because you are real men and all real men like to fight. When you, here, everyone of you, were kids, you all admired the champion marble player, the fastest runner, the toughest boxer, the big league ball players, and the All-American football players. Americans love a winner. Americans will not tolerate a loser. Americans despise cowards. Americans play to win all of the time. I wouldn’t give a hoot in hell for a man who lost and laughed. That’s why Americans have never lost nor will ever lose a war; for the very idea of losing is hateful to an American.

The young soldiers sat in rapt attention. They were listening to a legend. Thus far in the Second World War, Patton had commanded US Western Task Forces in Operation Torch, invading French Morocco and capturing Casablanca. He rejuvenated a beleaguered Tunisia campaign, turning demoralizing defeat into scintillating victory. Patton successfully invaded Sicily. And he engaged in elaborate subterfuge to draw the Germans away from the Normandy invasion point. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

On the other hand, the soldiers before him had been well-trained. They had engaged in exhausting maneuvers in Louisiana and grueling exercises in the Mojave Desert. They were fit. They were prepared. And they were enormously inexperienced. “You are not all going to die,” Patton pronounced. 

Only two percent of you right here today would die in a major battle. Death must not be feared. Death, in time, comes to all men. Yes, every man is scared in his first battle. If he says he’s not, he’s a liar. Some men are cowards but they fight the same as the brave men or they get the hell slammed out of them watching men fight who are just as scared as they are. The real hero is the man who fights even though he is scared. Some men get over their fright in a minute under fire. For some, it takes an hour. For some, it takes days. But a real man will never let his fear of death overpower his honor, his sense of duty to his country, and his innate manhood. Battle is the most magnificent competition in which a human being can indulge. It brings out all that is best and it removes all that is base. Americans pride themselves on being He Men and they ARE He Men. Remember that the enemy is just as frightened as you are, and probably more so. They are not supermen.

The soldiers smiled and sat a little taller. Their foreboding about the godlike Hitler, the ruthless SS, the unrelenting Wehrmacht, and the ideology of the master-race shrank as Patton strutted and spat and knifed his crop through the air. They may be inexperienced, but they know where they came from and who they were fighting for. Many men came from blue-collar or no-collar families. They grew up going to Mass, playing baseball in the vacant lot, working a lot while earning a little. They were young men of the Great Depression whose dads struggled for work and whose mothers repurposed leftovers, darned socks, and made soap. There wasn’t much, but there was God and family. As G. K. Chesterton once asserted, “The true soldier fights not because he hates what is in front of him but because he loves what is behind him.”

“There are four hundred neatly marked graves somewhere in Sicily all because one man went to sleep on the job.” Patton grew silent and then men leaned forward, “But they are German graves, because we caught the bastards asleep before they did. An Army is a team. It lives, sleeps, eats, and fights as a team. This individual heroic stuff is pure horse—t.”

Later, Patton would add,

One of the bravest men that I ever saw was a fellow on top of a telegraph pole in the midst of a furious fire fight in Tunisia. I stopped and asked what the hell he was doing up there at a time like that. He answered, “Fixing the wire, Sir.” I asked, “Isn’t that a little unhealthy right about now?” He answered, “Yes Sir, but the G—damned wire has to be fixed.” I asked, “Don’t those planes strafing the road bother you?” And he answered, “No, Sir, but you sure as hell do!” Now, there was a real man. A real soldier. There was a man who devoted all he had to his duty, no matter how seemingly insignificant his duty might appear at the time, no matter how great the odds.

Peppered in at one point or another, Patton reminded,

I want you to remember that no poor bastard ever won a war by dying for his country. He won it by making the other poor dumb son-of-a-b— bastard die for his country. Remember that.

This is what the soldiers knew, but needed to hear. We fight as one. We do not quit. We do the hard thing because no one else will. And then we win. “There is one great thing that you men will all be able to say after this war is over and you are home once again.” Patton’s iron jaw finally broke into a broad smile. 

You may be thankful that twenty years from now when you are sitting by the fireplace with your grandson on your knee and he asks you what you did in the great World War II, you WON’T have to cough, shift him to the other knee and say, “Well, your Granddaddy shoveled sh-t in Louisiana.” No, Sir, you can look him straight in the eye and say, “Son, your Granddaddy rode with the Great Third Army and a Son-of-a-G—damned-B—h named Georgie Patton!”

The men stood. And roared. And saluted.

Not long after D-Day, the Third Army’s Sixth Armored Division would land on Utah Beach and create a notable breakout at Avranches. Later, they would come to the rescue of besieged American forces around Bastogne during the Battle of the Bulge. After that, they would cross the Rhine River into the heart of Germany and, ultimately, liberate 21,000 prisoners from the hellscape of Buchenwald concentration camp.

At just the right moment, it took a complicated figure like Gen. George S. Patton to remind uncertain soldiers embarking on a harrowing campaign of who they are and not simply what they should do.

Today, we thank all veterans—for giving their freedom to protect ours, for living with honor to preserve ours, for enduring the darkness so we may live in the light. 

Thank you for teaching us what we should do.

Even more, thank you for reminding us of just who we are.

items.title: Our Modern Goetheian Deal with the Devil
items.author: Casey Chalk
items.summary:
Casey Chalk

As the worldview underlying Goethe’s “Faust” shows, modern man has traded his soul for prizes far less fabulous than one might expect.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Casey Chalk

The proverbial “deal with the devil” is typically understood as trading one’s soul for some great gift or experience. The great bluesman Robert Johnson, so the story goes, learned his guitar skills “down at the crossroads,” from “Old Scratch,” and paid for it by dying on his hands and knees, barking like a dog. Oscar Wilde’s titular character Dorian Gray makes a bargain to remain young and beautiful for the sake of a life of libertinism but ends up committing suicide. And, made famous by English playwright Christopher Marlow and later by German polymath Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Dr. Faust (or Faustus) bargains with the demonic Mephistopheles to procure a moment of this-worldly bodily and intellectual transcendence.

We are familiar with the cautionary lesson to be learned: Whatever great benefit may come from the immoral shortcut—of which the bargain with Satan is but the most extreme example—it will in the end bring us ruin. All the glory and pleasure will soon evaporate, and we’ll be left with the terrible, sometimes even deadly, consequences of our short-sighted avarice and lust. But in truth, the devil is rarely so dramatic. As the worldview underlying Goethe’s Faust shows, modern man has traded his soul for prizes far less fabulous than one might expect.

When we first meet Faust, he is a brilliant scholar who, though he has mastered much learning, remains deeply dissatisfied. Professional achievement, philosophy, and even conventional religion all fail to generate the fullness of life for which he yearns. He can “hear the message” of the Gospel at Easter, but he can “believe no longer.” What Faust desires is, “a vision of Nature’s forces; That bind the world, all its seeds and sources; And innermost life—all this I shall see.” He aspires to experience everything—to penetrate the secrets of existence, to overcome his limitations, and attain a deeper sense of knowledge and fulfillment.

Unbeknownst to him, Mephistopheles (in a literary allusion to the Book of Job) is discussing the discouraged Faust with God above. Yet, argues scholar and translator David Luke, Mephistopheles is “neither Milton’s nor Marlowe’s Devil,” but is rather “de-theologized.” There is (seemingly intentionally) no reference to sin, evil, hell, or damnation, and even death is dismissed by the devil, who declares that he is indifferent to what happens to men after they die. 

The Lord, alternatively, is not so much the God of the Bible but a spokesman of Goethe’s “positive and life-affirming” Romanticism. He is proud of Faust, whom, he asserts, “serves me, but still serves me in confusion; I will soon lead him into clarity. A gardener knows, one day this young green tree; Will blossom and bear fruit in rich profusion.” 

Goethe thus subverts the classic drama of the battle over men’s souls and in its place presents to us a more modern dichotomy: human striving versus hopelessness. Mephistopheles, who is given divine permission to tempt Faust, is intended to manifest genuine, objective despair and the idea that human imperfection invalidates human aspiration, while Faust represents the subjective despair even the idealist often feels. God, in turn, is the realization and embodiment of that hopeful idealism. “Man errs as long as he strives,” Goethe has the Lord declare, neatly summarizing Goethe’s positive view of humanity.

When Mephistopheles (first in the form of a dog and then as himself) arrives at Faust’s home, he tempts the scholar in words that will appeal to him: “My friend, you shall in this one night, In this one hour, know greater sensuous delight; Than in a whole monotonous year!” Though he first demurs, eventually Faust gives in:

Books sicken me, I’ll learn no more. Now let us slake hot passions in; The depths of sweet and sensual Sin! Make me your magics—I’ll not care to know; What lies behind their outward show.” He desires, “To give oneself entirely and to feel; Ecstasy that must last for ever! For ever!—For its end would be despair. No, never-ending! Never ending!

With Mephistopheles’s help, he seduces the poor maiden Gretchen (also referred to as Margarete). Yet in short order, their romantic fling becomes all consuming, and in order to preserve the lovers’ privacy, Gretchen murders her mother with a sleeping potion. After she becomes pregnant, her brother challenges Faust to a duel, and, again with Mephistopheles’s assistance, the brother is killed. Gretchen then murders her newborn child and is sent to prison. Faust attempts to free her from the dungeon, but she, having accepted her fate, refuses, while heavenly voices announce her salvation. Thus concludes Part One; in the (less widely-read) second part, Faust seeks to redeem himself by doing good for the world and future generations. “Whoever strives with all his might, we can redeem” sing the angelic hosts who guide him to his heavenly reward.

Despite the religious imagery, this is far from a traditional Christian story. Faust, writes Luke, is representative of a de-Christianized Romanticism, “something like a myth of European man.” The titular character does not appear to believe in God. When Gretchen speaks to him of God, Faust replies: “My dear, how can Anyone dare to say: I believe in Him? Ask a priest how, ask a learned man, And all their answers merely seem; To mock the questioner.” His quest for “God,” as such, is not spiritual or transcendent but earthly and to be realized through the natural order and earthly experience, striving, however imperfectly, to do good and be happy. 

“Weimar Classicism was, in sophisticated and non-trivial senses, idealistic and optimistic, as well as humanistic in the sense that it saw the world anthropocentrically rather than theologically, and in the sense that it took a positive, indeed Pelagian view of human nature and human potential,” writes Luke. In Goethe, there is no original sin from which man must be redeemed by divine, salvific grace. Faust, in Luke’s words, is “saved by the organic development of his own righteousness.” (Helmuth Kiesel in a 2019 article in the German theological journal Communio makes much the same point.)

In this psychological humanism, Goethe quite effectively seemed to presage modern man. Today, the moral vision of the secular West excludes God (or, like Goethe, defines him as a benevolent, almost impersonal force who is simply happy to see us trying). Our conception of the good life, in turn, increasingly elides classical virtue in favor of therapeutic self-optimization and self-help, obsessed with health, longevity, and the latest “life hack.” We define goodness not by conformity to a received, objective moral order, obedience to divine law, or the achievement of a particular virtue, but by an ongoing process of effort and self-development—what F. J. Lamport describes in his essay on Goethe as a “perfectibilism” that identifies striving as the true telos of man.

Yet, pace Goethe, what if that perfectibilism is the actual deal with the devil—one in which men forget their divine origin and end in favor of trite celebrations of simply finding your “best self,” and “living your best life” through this-worldly pleasures and experiences? Created for virtue, holiness, and eternal life with God, we limit our horizons to the banal and mundane. Modern man, like Goethe’s Faust, is justified not through the grace of a God who descends from heaven and through his sacrificial death secures our salvation, but by self-satisfying canards about being a “good person” and having the right opinions, proudly displayed via bumper stickers, yard signs, and social media posts.

C. S. Lewis in The Weight of Glory cautions us regarding such a myopic worldview: 

Our Lord finds our desires, not too strong, but too weak. We are half-hearted creatures, fooling about with drink and sex and ambition when infinite joy is offered us, like an ignorant child who wants to go on making mud pies in a slum because he cannot imagine what is meant by the offer of a holiday at the sea. We are far too easily pleased.

This is the Faustian bargain of prosperous modernity. We expect the devil to appear in smoke and fire, proffering his wears with a ghoulish smile. But perhaps, like Faust, the true devilry is in settling for an emotive “authenticity” and “living intentionally.” As he invitingly sings: “Oh, fill your heart right up with all of this, And when you’re brimming over with the bliss; Of such a feeling, call it what you like! Call it joy, or your heart, or love, or God! I have no name for it. The feeling’s all there is.” But, in truth, this will not bring us salvation. We were made for more than this.
